question: Solve the question and explain it using the digrams by redrawing them

slides.title: Coaxial capacitor: longitudinal view
slides.caption: x=R,\qquad a=\sqrt{2}R,\qquad b=2R
slides.narration: The question asks for the electric-field flux through the plane x=R inside a coaxial capacitor. We first redraw the longitudinal geometry and mark the plane whose normal points in the positive x direction.

slides.title: Cross-section and contributing segments
slides.caption: x=R,\qquad R\leq |y|\leq\sqrt{3}R
slides.bridge: Now view the same setup end-on.
slides.narration: In cross-section, the conductors are concentric circles and the plane becomes the line x=R. Only the two symmetric segments between the inner and outer radii lie in the dielectric and contribute to the flux.

slides.title: Dielectric endpoints
slides.caption: R\leq |y|\leq\sqrt{3}R
slides.bridge: Intersecting the two circles gives the endpoints.
slides.narration: Substituting x=R into the circular boundaries gives y=\pm R at the inner conductor and y=\pm\sqrt{3}R at the outer conductor. Thus two symmetric segments of the plane lie in the dielectric.

slides.title: Gaussian cylinder in the dielectric
slides.caption: \oint\mathbf D\cdot d\mathbf A=Q,\qquad D(2\pi r\ell)=Q
slides.bridge: The contributing pieces now determine the field.
slides.narration: We redraw the Gaussian cylinder coaxially inside the dielectric. Cylindrical symmetry makes the displacement field radial and constant on the curved surface, so Gauss's law gives D times 2 pi r ell equal to Q.

slides.title: Field in dielectric
slides.caption: \mathbf E(r)=\frac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0\kappa\ell r}\,\hat{\mathbf r}
slides.bridge: Gauss's law gives the radial field.
slides.narration: Gauss's law gives D=Q/(2\pi r\ell). Using \mathbf D=\varepsilon_0\kappa\mathbf E introduces the factor 1/(\varepsilon_0\kappa) in the electric field.

slides.title: Normal component
slides.caption: E_x=\frac{QR}{2\pi\varepsilon_0\kappa\ell(R^2+y^2)}
slides.bridge: The plane needs the normal component, not the full field.
slides.narration: Flux uses the component normal to the plane, not the full radial field. At (R,y), the radial unit vector has x-component R/r, producing the stated E_x.

slides.title: Both segments
slides.caption: \Phi_E=2\ell\int_R^{\sqrt{3}R}\frac{Q R}{2\pi\varepsilon_0\kappa\ell(R^2+y^2)}\,dy
slides.bridge: Add the equal upper and lower contributions.
slides.narration: A strip has area dA=\ell\,dy. The upper and lower dielectric segments contribute equally because E_x depends on y^2, so one integral is multiplied by two.

slides.title: Angular integral
slides.caption: \int_R^{\sqrt{3}R}\frac{R\,dy}{R^2+y^2}=\frac{\pi}{12}
slides.narration: The integral is an angular change in disguise. Its endpoint angles are \pi/3 and \pi/4, so the angular difference is \pi/12.

slides.title: Simplify flux
slides.caption: \Phi_E=\frac{Q}{12\varepsilon_0\kappa}
slides.narration: Substituting the angular integral cancels the cylinder length and the factor of \pi. The general electric-field flux is Q/(12\varepsilon_0\kappa).

slides.title: Insert kappa
slides.caption: \kappa=5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\Phi_E=\frac{Q}{60\varepsilon_0}
slides.narration: For this dielectric, \kappa=5. With Q positive and the normal directed toward increasing x, the flux is positive.

slides.title: Flux and units
slides.caption: \Phi_E=\frac{Q}{60\varepsilon_0}
slides.bridge: This is electric-field flux, not displacement flux.
slides.narration: Do not confuse electric-field flux with displacement flux. The requested quantity is \Phi_E, with units of newton metre squared per coulomb; reversing the normal reverses its sign.

slides.title: Final answer
slides.caption: \boxed{\Phi_E=\frac{Q}{60\varepsilon_0}}
slides.narration: Therefore, for the plane at x=R and the +\hat{\mathbf x} normal, the electric-field flux is Q/(60\varepsilon_0). Reversing the normal changes the sign.
